These experiences have influenced their approach to employment. They prefer financial security over status games. The gig economy (e.g., Uber) and the platform economy (e.g., Upwork) made them comfortable with having multiple jobs rather than relying on a single income source.

Gen-Z is proficient in technology, often automating tasks more efficiently than older generations. They also prefer digital communication and immediate feedback, valuing real-time discussions over long, formal reviews. To manage this new workforce effectively, engineering leaders must focus on creating environments that support flexibility, clear communication, and opportunities for professional development — all while fostering a sense of mission and purpose within the team.

One key insight here is that Gen-Z’s expectations for work-life balance are more pronounced than previous generations. They value clear boundaries between work and personal time and prioritize mental health. This suggests that leaders who foster a supportive, balanced, and inclusive work culture will likely attract and retain top talent from this generation.

Do you want more? For some insights and hints, you can read my article: How to Manage Gen-Z

When the pandemic locked us in our homes, many thought that 2020 would begin a truly remote-first world. Today, almost five years later, with companies like Amazon mandating a return to in-person work in 2025, the debate over remote versus office work has resurfaced.

The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated globalization and remote work. Coding languages and software design patterns are universal globally, meaning engineers can write the same code for an overseas employer and earn twice as much.

On the other hand, companies can hire less expensive specialists from less developed countries. For example, shifting a dev team from the Bay Area to Poland reduced costs by 40% while maintaining performance.

But it’s not always about money. Amazon’s stance is that in-office collaboration fosters better innovation, culture, and learning. However, the question remains whether this decision represents a step backward, especially for tech workers who thrived in remote-first environments during the pandemic.

The pandemic showed us how teams can function effectively remotely, but it also highlighted the limitations of remote work, such as the lack of nonverbal communication cues and the blurring of work-life boundaries. In many ways, engineering teams are naturally suited to remote work—most of our tools and processes have long been remote-friendly. However, office environments can still play a key role in fostering collaboration and cultural alignment, which are harder to achieve in fully remote settings.

Studies show that remote workers can be more productive than their office counterparts. For example, Stanford University research found that remote workers were 9% more productive than office workers, according to Psychology Today.

Another study reveals that out of an 8-hour day, the average worker is productive for only 3 hours. For the remaining time, they read the news, browse social media, search for new jobs, or discuss non-work-related topics with co-workers.

Here’s the dilemma: As a leader, do you want your people onsite, available for 8 hours but only working effectively for half that time and slacking for the rest? Or do you want them to be slightly more productive but out of your direct control?

As an engineering leader, the focus should be on outcomes, not just hours spent. Hybrid models, where teams come together for strategic meetings but remain remote for focused work, seem to balance individual flexibility and collective creativity.

Ultimately, organizations must assess whether their teams’ productivity and culture benefit more from in-person presence or if remote work can continue to support their goals.

If you want to explore more in the debate on Office vs. Remote, check my latest newsletter issue: Why Do Companies Drag Us Back to the Office?.

I’ve also shared some tips on How to Build Remote-First Culture.

Quality Assurance practices in software engineering have shifted significantly in recent years, with many organizations moving away from hiring dedicated testers to a QA shift-left approach. This means integrating testing responsibilities into the role of software engineers.

Companies like Microsoft retired their Software Development Engineer in Test roles nearly a decade ago, opting to merge testing and development functions.

Main reasons for doing so were challenges many of us know:

  • Who should write unit tests — engineers or testers?
  • “Us vs. them” dynamics, with differing goals, schedules, QA gatekeeping, and “ticket ping-pong.”
  • Complex testing systems that still required senior engineering help.
  • Inverted testing pyramid with the majority of heavy E2E tests.

The rise of DevOps and continuous delivery models lead to faster and more automated testing processes. Manual testing simply cannot keep up with the pace of modern software delivery, where top-performing teams deploy code multiple times a day with low failure rates.

In this environment, quality is no longer something that gets “checked” after development; it is embedded throughout the entire software delivery process.

One critical insight here is that this trend is part of a broader movement toward DevOps culture, where the lines between development and operations blur.

According to the DORA 2023 Research, the highest-performing organizations deploy code 46 times more frequently and have 2,555 times faster lead times than low performers. Automated tests and rapid feedback loops are key drivers behind this success, which is why engineering teams must embrace testing as part of their development responsibilities.

Engineering leaders must now ensure that their teams are equipped with the tools and knowledge to own the quality of their code. Automated testing, CI/CD pipelines, and real-time feedback loops are critical in achieving faster, more reliable releases.

So, what happens to testers who may become redundant? Such transformations don’t occur overnight and often take months or years to phase out the QA team, providing ample time to rethink the role’s future.

Manual testers often transition to QA engineers, automating work that takes hours into scripts executed in minutes. Their role may then evolve into that of an evangelist or agent of change, creating solutions (templates, infrastructure) that all engineers can use. They ensure every developer knows how to run tests and can do so in minutes.

Over time, it may become infrastructure engineering work. For example, optimizing CI/CD pipelines to cut testing execution time by sharding and parallelizing tests. (A few years ago, one of my teams reduced execution time from a few hours to less than 30 minutes by moving testing infrastructure to cloud solutions).

Wait… does this mean a QA Engineer becomes a Software Engineer?

In short, yes. Many QA engineers already do engineering work: writing scripts, setting up testing infrastructure, building automated pipelines — it’s code development. Yet many organizations keep dedicated QA Engineer roles, often paying them 50% to 70% of an engineer’s salary and expecting less from them than from regular engineers (you are good at writing automations but not so good at writing production code).

To explore more, check my newsletter issue: Do You Need More Testers or Better Tests?

Another notable trend is the reduced demand for engineering managers. With tech companies facing budget cuts and flattening hierarchies, there has been a shift toward hiring individual contributors over managers.

For example, in his letter, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy noted,

“we’re asking each S-team organization to increase the ratio of individual contributors to managers by at least 15% by the end of Q1 2025. Having fewer managers will remove layers and flatten organizations more than they are today.”

Does this mean that management is obsolete? I think it’s rather a focus on having better engineering managers, not necessarily more of them.

Here are the top sins of engineering leaders:

  • Micromanaging — merely assigning tasks, not allowing collective decision-making, and not building overall awareness of why their engineers do what they do (reminder: the role of technology in a product company is to solve customers’ problems).
  • Not contributing to product discovery — the role of engineering is not only about delivering features. It’s also about discovering the best way to solve customer problems.
  • Not being hands-on — it’s not just about contributing to code development. Being hands-on also means stepping into an engineer’s shoes — understanding their real struggles, developer experience, etc.
  • Not managing expectations — a semi-annual performance review is not enough. Engineering leaders must constantly work on course correction, growing teams’ skillsets, and finding the most impactful initiatives for their people.
  • Being gatekeepers, not enablers — rather than finding a solution or trying to better understand the problem, they “protect” the team until they get 100% of the requirements for the work to be done.

Today’s engineering managers are expected to be more hands-on, contributing directly to the team’s output while also handling leadership responsibilities. According to DORA research, organizations with transformational leadership — where leaders are both visionaries and hands-on — are more likely to achieve high performance.

Leaders who can effectively manage talent, set clear goals, and align technology with business strategy will be indispensable, even in leaner organizational structures. The focus is now on outcomes — helping teams deliver value to customers, rather than just completing tasks.

For a deeper analysis, check my blog post:

The role of technology in a product company is to solve customers’ problems. Engineering is not a cost center but a profit center. Software engineers don’t work for the Product team; they are part of the Product team.

All of these statements emphasize that our focus should be shifted from building code to building products. It shouldn’t be a surprise — with high-level programming languages, no-code solutions, generative AI, and mature frameworks, it’s easier than ever before to build fully working solutions.

Transforming engineering teams to operate within a product-centric model is not just a shift in processes — it’s a change in mindset. As engineering leaders, our role is to ensure that we are not just building more efficiently but also solving the right problems and making strategic decisions that align with the overall product vision.

There are a few key principles that help with that, focusing on:

  • Changing the way things are built through frequent, small releases, product instrumentation, monitoring, staged rollout & early validation.
  • Changing the way problems are solved through being aware that the “requirements” are hypotheses; being a partner to the Product organization who helps with finding solutions, not just points out gaps in their reasoning; translating “technical” problems into true business value and prioritizing them along with other product tasks; taking part in the discovery process where ideas are validated much quicker.
  • Changing the way decisions are made about which problems to solve through building awareness that an engineering leader is a product leader too, so we contribute to product roadmaps; ensuring that engineering teams know and understand the product vision; focusing engineering teams on outcomes, not features to build; building engineers’ awareness of customers and users and collecting qualitative feedback.

For specific actions and an overview of the book where the concept of the Product Operating Model was introduced, I invite you to my previous blog post:

The software engineering landscape is shifting, and as leaders, it’s crucial to stay ahead of these trends. Whether it’s adapting to a new generation of workers, navigating the remote vs. in-office debate, evolving QA practices, or refining management styles, engineering leaders must embrace change while maintaining focus on the key goal: delivering products that solve real customer problems.

Those who can adapt and guide their teams through these transitions will thrive in the decade to come.

As we move forward, the role of engineering leadership will continue to evolve, but one thing remains clear: leaders who prioritize outcomes over processes, foster a collaborative team culture, and embrace technological and generational shifts will be best equipped to navigate the challenges ahead.

I have a quick announcement.

On October 21st, I’m launching “Better Engineering Leader,” a free-of-charge email daily course that distills two years of writing from Practical Engineering Management into a focused, six-week journey.

If you want to join, check details about the course here: Be Better Engineering Leader Ahead of 2025

You can also explore more content for engineering managers on practicalengineering.management. You will find practical strategies for effective engineering leadership.

Join the community of impactful leaders to bridge the gap between inspiration and implementation with actionable steps that empower your team, boost trust, and drive real-world results.

If you would like to discuss any of your challenges, don’t hesitate to reach out to me at mirek@practicalengineering.management.

item.title: The New Claude 3.5 Sonnet Is Lazy When Given Large Context
item.description:
Score 2 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @vincent_s
October 28, 2024 | https://www.vincentschmalbach.com/the-new-claude-3-5-sonnet-is-lazy-when-given-large-context/ | archive.org

I've noticed a significant issue with Anthropic's latest Claude 3.5 Sonnet model: it becomes increasingly lazy as conversation context grows.

This is a consistent pattern where the model's willingness to complete tasks deteriorates with each addition to the conversation history.

The Pattern

The degradation follows a clear trajectory. Early in a conversation, Claude 3.5 Sonnet works as expected, generating complete responses and fulfilling tasks efficiently. But as context accumulates, it starts exhibiting increasingly "lazy" behaviors:

  1. First, it begins breaking content into smaller chunks
  2. Then it starts adding "[Continue with...]" placeholders
  3. Later, it constantly asks for permission to continue
  4. Finally, it reaches peak laziness - responding with nothing but: 
    [Would you like me to proceed with the complete article content now?]

    (Without giving me the actual article or even parts of it.)

item.title: Why Google Search Is Falling Apart?
item.description:
Score 14 | Comments 15 (thread link) | @akm24
October 28, 2024 | https://wpxplore.com/google-search-is-falling-apart/ | archive.org

Listen To The Podcast on This Article

Google Search has long been the most reliable way to find information online. But recently, users have noticed things changing—and not for the better. Why Google Search is Falling Apart? With more ads, misleading design, and questionable results, many users wonder if the platform prioritizes profit over usability. Let’s break it down.

Google dominates the global search market with a 91.47% share, including a 95.32% share on mobile and 81.95% on desktop

Reasons Why Google Search is Falling Apart

Google Search has been a dominant tool for finding information, but it’s showing signs of decline. Here are the main reasons why Google Search is falling apart:

1. Ad overload: Too many Ads, not enough information

  • Four or more ads take up the top of the results page, forcing you to scroll to find organic results.
  • The increased number of ads can push the information you need far down the page.
  • This prioritization of paid content can make finding relevant, unbiased information frustrating.

2. The “Fold Factor”: Hidden information below the Fold

  • Think of the “fold” of a newspaper as the area visible before opening.
  • For that, the “fold” refers to the part of the search results page that is visible without scrolling. Ads now often occupy this space, pushing organic results down.
  • Important content often gets buried beneath ads, forcing users to scroll further than expected.

3. Misleading design: Blurring the line between Ads and organic results

  • Google used to mark sponsored ads with a yellow background, but now it’s gone.
  • Today, sponsored results blend in with organic ones, making it hard to distinguish between paid and organic content.
  • This design change makes users more likely to click on ads without realizing it, potentially leading to less relevant or commercialized results.

4. Questionable shopping results: Overcrowded with Ads

  • Product searches bring up a carousel of shopping ads, often for products unrelated to your search.
  • These ads are often paid placements; some may even direct you to low-quality or scam websites.
  • Instead of seeing helpful product reviews or comparisons, you’re faced with ads that need to be more transparent about the search experience.

5. Ads vs. accuracy: Irrelevant results take over

  • Search queries like “thinnest mini fridge” might return ads that are totally unrelated to what you’re looking for.
  • Organic search results are often overshadowed by paid promotions, making it harder to find accurate information.
  • Google’s emphasis on ads over relevance can lead to a frustrating user experience.

6. The impact of SEO tactics

  • SEO (Search Engine Optimization) has become more complex, with website owners using a variety of tactics to improve rankings.
  • Some websites use keyword stuffing or over-optimize content with keywords, which leads to low-quality or irrelevant content appearing higher in search results.
  • This manipulation of SEO can degrade the user experience, as it prioritizes content that isn’t necessarily the best or most accurate but well-optimized.

7. The role of AI in search

  • Google has increasingly integrated Generative AI (GI) or Artificial Intelligence (AI) into its search algorithms to refine results.
  • While AI can improve the relevance of search results, it also introduces new challenges:
    • AI-generated content is becoming harder to distinguish from human-generated content, potentially flooding search results with less valuable or authentic content.
    • AI algorithms may have biases, resulting in biased or unbalanced search results based on their training and the data they are given.

8. The future of search

  • The future of search is uncertain as Google continues to evolve its algorithms and integrate emerging technologies like AI.
  • As these changes unfold, users can expect the search experience to shift significantly in the coming years.
  • Users must stay aware of these shifts, remain critical of search results, and explore alternative search engines.

What’s Causing the Decline?

The answer lies in Google’s business model:

  • Google’s primary revenue source is advertising, which encourages the platform to push ads more aggressively.
  • The more users click on ads, the more money Google earns—but at the expense of user satisfaction.
  • As a result, Google is focusing more on ad revenue than user experience.

Is There a Fix?

Here are a few potential solutions:

  • User Feedback: If enough people voice their dissatisfaction, Google may consider making changes to balance ads with user experience.
  • Explore Alternatives: Consider using other search engines like:
    • DuckDuckGo: Focuses on privacy and ad-free experiences.
    • Ecosia: A search engine that plants trees with its revenue.
    • Bing: Often overlooked, but provides a clean and ad-light experience.

In 2024, 77% of individuals use Google for online searches more than three times a day

Final Note

If you’ve noticed a decline in the quality of Google Search, you’re not alone. It’s important to be aware of these changes and adjust how you navigate the platform. Take action:

  • Share your feedback with Google to encourage improvements.
  • Explore other search engines that better suit your accurate and ad-free information needs.

Stay informed, stay critical, and always seek the best search experience!

FAQs – Google Search is Falling Apart

1. Why is Google Search showing more ads?

Google prioritizes ads in search results as part of its revenue model, increasing visible advertisements.

2. What is keyword stuffing?

Keyword stuffing is an SEO tactic where websites overuse keywords to manipulate search rankings, often resulting in low-quality content.

3. How does AI affect Google Search results?

AI is used to refine search algorithms but can also introduce biases and make AI-generated content hard to distinguish from human-generated content.

4. What is the “fold” in search results?

The “fold” refers to the part of the search results page that is visible without scrolling. Ads now often occupy this space, pushing organic results down.

5. What can users do if they find Google Search unreliable?

Users can provide feedback to Google and explore alternative search engines for better experiences.

6. How does SEO manipulation affect search quality?

Manipulative SEO tactics can lead to irrelevant or low-quality content ranking higher in search results, degrading the overall user experience.

7. What might the future hold for Google Search?

As Google continues to evolve its algorithms and incorporate new technologies, the search experience may change significantly, requiring users to adapt.

item.title: Scheduling Model in LLVM – Part II
Are Inboxes Evil?
item.description:
Score 2 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @_bramses
October 28, 2024 | https://www.bramadams.dev/issue-59-are-inboxes-evil/ | archive.org

< Previous Issue

If you want to make a knowledge worker instinctually tense up, a good place to start is by reminding them of their (likely overflowing) inbox.

"Inbox" has become a bad word of sorts, something that one mustn't bring up in polite conversation. An inbox is a reminder of work undone, obligations unfulfilled, a miasma of past, present, and future stressors.

But why is this the case? Are inboxes deserving of their bad reputation?

An inbox is a queue. This queue largely has two features:

  1. Allow information to be dealt with asynchronously (aka at some arbitrary time in the future)
  2. Prioritize said information

On the face of it these features are genuinely helpful, or at worst, inert. In theory, being able to reply to a message later frees us to stay focused on our current task. And in theory, having a priority queue enabled in our system allows us to filter out noise, and only focus on high ROI communication.

In theory, that is.

In practice, an inbox is an obligation. An inbox is an obligation – ironically – because of the features that make a queue useful. The asynchronous information allows senders to barrage an inbox while having no frame of reference whether their receiver is overloaded. The priority list ranks back-and-forth conversations aggressively, leading to multiple threads of email hot potato taking up the top spots in the queue.

In practice, the email inbox is a system where the more effort you put in, the more work arrives later. In other words, the better you are at email, the more email you are expected to answer. Sucks, right?

To deal with foreign systems, individuals must enact systems of their own as preventive mechanisms. While there are many good systems for dealing with email inboxes, I'll only highlight one. Then I'll close out by talking about a strategy that I think makes dealing with inboxes in general more palatable.

Office Hours is a concept that prevents items from being added to your queue in the first place by setting up the following conditions:

  1. I am available from the window of X-Y, where you can receive an immediate reply
  2. Outside of office hours, you can contact me with important information through some non-trivial route (in 2024, something as simple as a phone call is often too much for people to go through with, so this is good)

The office hours method is great because it solves both problems the inbox introduces. It gives our senders a chance to ask their question and know they'll get a reply, and the sender will be able to see if you are – or aren't – bandwidth locked.

I personally take office hour calls Tuesday, and then have recently been doing a livestream office hour session on Fridays.

The office hours technique is amazing, but at the end of the day, it is merely a technique.

For the inbox in general, I think we need to do better. Strategies will only take us so far. In order to conquer our inbox, we must think bigger than workarounds.

As mentioned prior, the inbox is a system unto itself. A combination of bad actors and downward societal pressures makes each individual inbox a slightly different version of hell. To get out means we must change the rules of play.

In 1894, a report by the state legislature found that New York was the densest city in the world, surpassing Paris, London, and Bombay, with the Lower East Side being the most densely populated place on the planet. In 1901, Theodore Roosevelt, then governor of New York, signed the Tenement House Act into law preventing tenement homes from being built in NYC.

113 years later, the Lower East Side (not without its problems, mind you), maintains its history while being one of the most attractive destinations to tourist and live on Earth. Changing the rules works.

It may seem farcical, but our inboxes can change as well. Allow me to add one feature to the specification I gave for an inbox above:

"This queue largely has

two

three features:"

  1. Allow information to be dealt with asynchronously (aka at some arbitrary time in the future)
  2. Prioritize said information
  3. Every manual effort put into the inbox improves the density and utility of the overall system

The third item isn't a feature that queues provide out the box, but is now technologically feasible thanks to advents in vector embeddings and Personal Library Science.

When you take action in an inbox, the system itself should compile that knowledge. This compilation of knowledge can show the user distant relationships from seemingly disparate sources of information – and more importantly – develop a cow pathing automaticity over time. Instead of an auto responder or a binary "mark as important flag", this third rule sits at the level below, organizing information in holistically useful manner for the owner of the inbox.

The third rule happens in the during and after of inbox processing, and informs future interaction, and is not technically concerned with delivery or prioritizing/filtering.

Allowing the inbox and owner to enter a mutualistic relationship means understanding what a queue is without judgment and asking if there are more effective ways of handling our communication streams, particularly at the level of the individual.

We can work towards a future by addressing the inbox at the system level and simultaneously decreasing the burden of the operator.

If done correctly, the stigma of an inbox will hopefully – slowly – loosen its grip on our collective psyche.

item.title: Go does what RxJS couldn't – a good way to handle state
item.description:
Score 2 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @thunderbong
October 28, 2024 | https://poxate.com/blog/go-does-what-rxjs-couldnt | archive.org

Imperative is a cookbook that instructs you to pour water, flower, and sugar into a bowl and mix it, before abruptly ending. You must find the rest of the instructions on another page titled, "addEventListener(ingredientsMixed)" on page 342, after they tell you about their cat that fell out the window in a jet heading for Honolulu.

On the other hand, RxJS is a thousand leaflets with a single instruction on top, then a ten links underneath.

Instruction: Check temperature when

  • Below 32°F (page 23) for [enter recipe]
  • Cake Rising rapidly (page 64)
  • Water Falling steadily (page 69)
  • Fluctuating (page 120)
  • Steady for 5 minutes (page 2)
  • Sudden drop (page 53)
  • Sudden spike (page 7)
  • Humidity above 80% (page 80)
  • Wind speed exceeds 20 mph? (page 192)

Finally, there's Go, a sane cook book that reads top-bottom in the order that instructions are executed, with the occasional inconvenience. It's not perfect, but it's a world ahead of RxJS and Imperative.

Don't believe me? Fine, you'll see it yourself along this multipart-series of "Overcoming State Management", where we build the world's most complicated playlist.

The application we are building is based on Prayershub, a all-in-one app for creating and sharing personalized worship sessions (with songs, psalms, and prayers), live broadcasting, and community engagement across multiple devices, all designed to enhance your spiritual journey.

Part 1.0 - What this series IS NOT

This series is

  • NOT a tutorial, plumbing work will not be shown
  • NOT a recommendation of Go
  • NOT a tutorial on RxJS or Go (we expect you to know these)

We are simply showcasing an approach to state management that most haven't heard of.

Part 1.1 - Setting the stage

Log everytime playBtn is clicked.

Note: GopherJS is used to integrate Go with JavaScript (not shown).

package main

func main() {
	p := NewPage()
	go p.StateManager()
}

func (p *Page) StateManager() {
	for {
		<-onClicked(p.playBtn)
		println("playBtn clicked")
	}
}

RxJS:

fromEvent(window.playBtn, "click").subscribe((_) => {
    console.log("playBtn clicked");
});

Imperative:

window.playBtn.addEventListener("click", () => {
    console.log("playBtn clicked");
});

Part 1.2 - Implementing the player

On playBtn clicked, toggle buttons and play each song in the playlist, one after another. In the end, toggle buttons to initial state.

In Go, it's pretty straightforward.

func (p *Page) StateManager() {
	for {
		// Note: `onClicked` returns a `chan struct{}`
		// that will emit a single value, then close
		<-onClicked(p.playBtn)
		
		hide(p.playBtn)
		show(p.pauseBtn, p.stopBtn)

		for _, song := range p.songs {
			song.Audio.Play()
			// wait for song to end
			<-song.Audio.Ended()
		}

		// When all songs have finished
		hide(p.pauseBtn, p.stopBtn)
		show(p.playBtn)
	}
}

With RxJS, there's no one way of doing that that makes everyone happy, so this must do. (For clarity, we are ignoring collecting all subscriptions in order to unsubscribe.)

const clickedPlay$ = fromEvent(window.playBtn, "click");

clickedPlay$.subscribe((_) => {
    hide(window.playBtn);
    show(window.pauseBtn, window.stopBtn);
});

// when last songs ends
fromEvent(songs[songs.length - 1].audio, "ended").subscribe((_) => {
    hide(window.pauseBtn, window.stopBtn);
    show(window.playBtn);
});

songs.forEach((song, index) => {
    const prevSong = songs[index - 1];

    // the first song plays on clickedPlay$
    // the others play when the previous song ends
    const shouldPlay$ = index == 0
        ? clickedPlay$
        : fromEvent(prevSong.audio, "ended");

    shouldPlay$.subscribe((_) => {
        song.audio.play();
    });
});

Then, finally, imperative:

window.playBtn.addEventListener("click", () => {
    songs[0].audio.play();
    hide(window.playBtn);
    show(window.pauseBtn, window.stopBtn);
});

songs.forEach((song, index) => {
    song.audio.addEventListener("ended", () => {
        const isLastSong = index == songs.length - 1;
        if (isLastSong) {
            hide(window.pauseBtn, window.stopBtn);
            show(window.playBtn);
        } else {
            songs[index + 1].audio.play();
        }
    });
});

Notice how the Imperative version has two places that call audio.play(), while the RxJS version only has one call. You'll see this pattern grow as we progress

Part 1.3 - Breaking control flow: Pause & Stop

On stopBtn clicked, stop all audios and return to normal state.

On pauseBtn, pause temporarily until resumeBtn clicked.

In Go, each song goes into an infinite blocking loop (songloop) that listens to pause, resume, stop, ended.

pause and resume pauses and resume, respectivly, then loop back into songloop

stop terminates songloop, reset current playing audio, and jumps back to mainloop

ended terminates songloop, but doesn't jump back to mainloop

func (p *Page) StateManager() {
	mainloop:
	for {
		<-onClicked(p.playBtn)
		hide(p.playBtn)
		show(p.pauseBtn, p.stopBtn)

		for _, song := range p.songs {
			song.Audio.Play()

			// infinitely loop until broken
			// by `stop` or `ended`
			songloop:
			for { 
				select {
				case <-onClicked(p.pauseBtn):
					song.Audio.Pause()
					hide(p.pauseBtn)
					show(p.resumeBtn)

				case <-onClicked(p.resumeBtn):
					song.Audio.Play()
					hide(p.resumeBtn)
					show(p.pauseBtn)

				case <-onClicked(p.stopBtn):
					song.Audio.Pause()
					song.Audio.SetTime(0)
					hide(p.stopBtn, p.pauseBtn, p.resumeBtn)
					show(p.playBtn)
					continue mainloop

				case <-song.Audio.Ended():
					break songloop
				}
			}
		}

		// When all songs have finished
		hide(p.pauseBtn, p.stopBtn)
		show(p.playBtn)
	}
}

At first, it seems Go won't continue scaling well as this application becomes more complicated, but looks can be deceiving.

Now, let's build an minimally viable RxJS version (after that, we'll do it idiomatically):

// we need to keep track of the current song
let currentSongIndex: number | null = null;

clickedPlay$.subscribe((_) => {
    hide(window.playBtn);
    show(window.pauseBtn, window.stopBtn);
});

clickedPause$.subscribe((_) => {
    hide(window.pauseBtn);
    show(window.resumeBtn);
    songs.forEach((song) => {
        song.audio.pause();
    });
});

clickedResume$.subscribe((_) => {
    hide(window.resumeBtn);
    show(window.pauseBtn);
    songs[currentSongIndex!].audio.play();
});

clickedStop$.subscribe((_) => {
    hide(window.stopBtn, window.pauseBtn, window.resumeBtn);
    show(window.playBtn);
    songs.forEach((song) => {
        song.audio.pause();
        song.audio.currentTime = 0;
    });
});

// when last songs ends
fromEvent(songs[songs.length - 1].audio, "ended").subscribe((_) => {
    hide(window.pauseBtn, window.stopBtn);
    show(window.playBtn);
});

songs.forEach((song, index) => {
    const prevSong = songs[index - 1];

    // the first song plays on clickedPlay$
    // the others play when the previous song ends
    const shouldPlay$ = index == 0
        ? clickedPlay$
        : fromEvent(prevSong.audio, "ended");

    shouldPlay$.subscribe((_) => {
       currentSongIndex = index;
        song.audio.play();
    });
});

Part 1.3.1 Idiotmatic RxJS

However, there's several glaring problems:

For one, there are serveral calls to show and hide buttons. How can you possibly track a bug with a button if everything is toggling their visibility?

Two, multiple places are calling audio.play(), we need to collocate all events that could play an audio.

Let's tackle the first one by breaking this up:

clickedPlay$.subscribe((_) => {
    hide(window.playBtn);
    show(window.pauseBtn, window.stopBtn);
});
// remove all hide() and show() calls

const showPlayBtn = clickedPlay$
    .pipe(map((_) => false))
    .subscribe((showBtn) => {
        if (showBtn) show(window.playBtn);
        else hide(window.playBtn);
    });

const showPauseBtn = clickedPlay$
    .pipe(map((_) => true))
    .subscribe((showBtn) => {
        if (showBtn) show(window.pauseBtn);
        else hide(window.pauseBtn);
    });

const showResumeBtn = clickedStop$
    .pipe(map((_) => true))
    .subscribe((showBtn) => {
        if (showBtn) show(window.resumeBtn);
        else hide(window.resumeBtn);
    });

const showStopBtn = clickedPlay$
    .pipe(map((_) => true))
    .subscribe((showBtn) => {
        if (showBtn) show(window.stopBtn);
        else hide(window.stopBtn);
    });

Don't scoff yet, complex tools look silly on simple problems. Let's extend each case. The app doesn't react to all changes yet (audio pauses, but no buttons are not toggled):

Here are the events that toggle show/hide for each button:

Let's implement in code:

const ended$ = merge(
    clickedStop$,
    fromEvent(songs[songs.length - 1].audio, "ended"),
);

const showPlayBtn = merge(
   clickedPlay$.pipe(map((_) => false)),
   ended$.pipe(map((_) => true)),
)
    .subscribe((showBtn) => {
        if (showBtn) show(window.playBtn);
        else hide(window.playBtn);
    });

const showPauseBtn = merge(
   clickedPlay$.pipe(map((_) => true)),
   clickedPause$.pipe(map((_) => false)),
   ended$.pipe(map((_) => false)),
)
    .subscribe((showBtn) => {
        if (showBtn) show(window.pauseBtn);
        else hide(window.pauseBtn);
    });

const showResumeBtn = merge(
   clickedPause$.pipe(map((_) => true)),
   clickedResume$.pipe(map((_) => false)),
   ended$.pipe(map((_) => false)),
)
    .subscribe((showBtn) => {
        if (showBtn) show(window.resumeBtn);
        else hide(window.resumeBtn);
    });

const showStopBtn = merge(
   clickedPlay$.pipe(map((_) => true)),
   ended$.pipe(map((_) => false)),
)
    .subscribe((showBtn) => {
        if (showBtn) show(window.stopBtn);
        else hide(window.stopBtn);
    });

Wait! There's a bug:

Problem: pauseBtn is not showing when pressing on resumeBtn

No problem, we can solve that easily:

const showPauseBtn = merge(
    clickedPlay$.pipe(map((_) => true)),
    clickedPause$.pipe(map((_) => false)),
   clickedResume$.pipe(map((_) => true)),
    ended$.pipe(map((_) => false)),
)
    .subscribe((showBtn) => {
        if (showBtn) show(window.pauseBtn);
        else hide(window.pauseBtn);
    });

Was this all worth it? Who knows?

Part 1.3.2 Audio handling

I'm not going to bother bringing through the same grueling process, so codedump:

// we need to keep track of the current song
let currentSongIndex: number | null = null;

clickedPause$.subscribe((_) => {
    songs.forEach((song) => {
        song.audio.pause();
    });
});

clickedResume$.subscribe((_) => {
    songs[currentSongIndex!].audio.play();
});

clickedStop$.subscribe((_) => {
    songs.forEach((song) => {
        song.audio.pause();
        song.audio.currentTime = 0;
    });
});

const currentItem$ = merge(
    ...songs.map((song, index) =>
        fromEvent(song.audio, "play")
            .pipe(map((_) => index))
    ),
    clickedStop$.pipe(map((_) => null)),
).pipe(startWith(null), shareReplay());

songs.forEach((song, songIndex) => {
    const prevSong = songs[songIndex - 1];

    merge(
        songIndex == 0
	        ? clickedPlay$
	        : fromEvent(prevSong.audio, "ended"),
        clickedResume$.pipe(
            withLatestFrom(currentItem$),
            filter(([_, currentItem]) => currentItem == songIndex),
        ),
    ).subscribe((_) => {
        song.audio.play();
    });

    merge(
        clickedPause$,
        clickedStop$,
    ).subscribe((_) => {
        song.audio.pause();
    });

    clickedStop$.subscribe((_) => {
        song.audio.currentTime = 0;
    });
});

First, it works, as far as anyone can tell.

Second, console.log is useless in a stream that is not share() or shareReplay()

Part 1.3.3 Imperative version

let currentItem: number | null = null;

window.playBtn.addEventListener("click", () => {
    currentItem = 0;

    songs[0].audio.play();
    hide(window.playBtn);
    show(window.pauseBtn, window.stopBtn);
});

window.pauseBtn.addEventListener("click", function () {
    songs.forEach((s) => s.audio.pause());
    hide(window.pauseBtn);
    show(window.resumeBtn);
});

window.resumeBtn.addEventListener("click", function () {
    songs[currentItem!].audio.play();
    hide(window.resumeBtn);
    show(window.pauseBtn);
});

window.stopBtn.addEventListener("click", function () {
    currentItem = 0;
    hide(window.stopBtn, window.pauseBtn, window.resumeBtn);
    show(window.playBtn);
    songs.forEach((s) => {
        s.audio.pause();
        s.audio.currentTime = 0;
    });
});

songs.forEach((song, index) => {
    song.audio.addEventListener("ended", () => {
        const playlistEnded = index == songs.length - 1;
        if (playlistEnded) {
            currentItem = null;
            hide(window.pauseBtn, window.resumeBtn, window.stopBtn);
            show(window.playBtn);
        } else {
            currentItem = index + 1;
            songs[index + 1].audio.play();
        }
    });
});

Notice how we must track currentItem in both RxJS and Imperative code in order to know which song to play when the resumeBtn is clicked.

We need not track this with Go, for as long as we remain inside an iteration, we know that's the current song we're playing:

func (p *Page) StateManager() {
mainloop:
	for {
		<-onClicked(p.playBtn)
		hide(p.playBtn)
		show(p.pauseBtn, p.stopBtn)

		for _, song := range p.songs {
			// as long as we are here
			// `song` is the current song
		}

		hide(p.pauseBtn, p.stopBtn)
		show(p.playBtn)
	}
}

Overview

We'll be building future parts of the world's most complicated playlist in future blog posts.

But for now, let's get a quick overview of the flow/state of the application in each example:

item.title: The Meaning of Wisdom
item.description:
Score 2 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @salomonk_mur
October 27, 2024 | https://www.salomonmuriel.com/posts/meaning-of-wisdom/ | archive.org

Wisdom by PhDs + Hundreds of strangers

I recently came across this article about the meaning of Wisdom. The researchers who came up with the meaning obtained it from what they call Experimental Philosophy, which basically means they asked many culturally and geographically diverse people for their personal meaning of this particular philosophical concept and then tried to gauge what the answers had in common.

Here’s exactly what they got:

There are two key characteristics. Reflective orientation is about people who think before acting, carefully consider different perspectives, and use logic and past experiences to guide their decisions. They’re the type of person who keeps their cool in difficult situations, taking time to weigh all the options before making a move.

The second is socio-emotional awareness. Wise people are good at understanding and caring about the thoughts and feelings of others. They pay attention to emotions and consider different views on the situation. Such an individual might be skilled at mediating conflicts by understanding each party’s point of view, or be adept at providing emotional support during difficult times.

Together, these two dimensions combine to form the global image of wisdom. The study suggests that the wisest people are those who balance both, showing strong abilities in reasoning while also being emotionally and socially aware.

As per this definition, I’m a very unwise person, given that I often value acting quickly instead of analyzing in depth. My constant decision to leave the premises immediately without checking if I’m carrying my bag/passport/phone/children would point in that direction too.

Wisdom for 3 year olds

The article struck a chord because I happen to be teaching a bit about Wisdom to my kids recently. There is this series of books called “Big Ideas for Little Philosophers” which present several concepts in a way that is accessible for children. They always start with a definition of Wisdom:

Who knew Socrates had such a zany dog?

According to this definition, knowing things that help you live better and happier is wisdom. But what kind of things? In this particular book, the examples are about how being truthful is the wise thing to do, even if it may not easy in many circumstances. Knowing how to act (like being truthful always) is what makes you wise.

Wisdom by nerds

The final definition that resonates with me is the one from Dungeons and Dragons. In the game, you define a character by 6 attributes, 3 physical and 3 mental. The mental attributes are Wisdom, Intelligence and Charisma, while the physical ones are Strength, Dexterity and Constitution.

The best example I’ve found describing these attributes is this 🍅

  • Strength is being able to crush a tomato.
  • Dexterity is being able to dodge a tomato.
  • Constitution is being able to eat a bad tomato.
  • Intelligence is knowing a tomato is a fruit.
  • Wisdom is knowing not to put a tomato in a fruit salad.
  • Charisma is being able to sell a tomato-based fruit salad.

Knowing how to apply your knowledge is wisdom. Meta-knowledge? This definition resonates the most with me (my nerd status notwithstanding).

Wisdom as accrued and varied knowledge

I believe Wisdom comes not from a method of doing things (as the PhDs define it), but from an accrual of knowledge (as the toddler books and D&D suggest). The method is just the result of the accrued knowledge: people who analyze decisions most likely have found over time that some time spent analyzing or trying to reach decisions that make people as happy as possible will lead to better results in the long run, and so they do it. But they are not wise because they exhibit those two behaviors; rather, they are wise because they have accrued knowledge that makes them act that way (and probably also makes them do a thousand other wise things, not reported in the study).

If this is true, then Wisdom is a skill that can only be acquired by living a broad range of experiences and learning about a broad range of topics. Knowing that a tomato doesn’t belong in a fruit salad is a result of knowing about both tomatoes and salads.

Another teaching in my kids’ book is that you should wonder at stuff everyday (such as what is wisdom, or anything else really). I think that nails the road towards Wisdom: If you keep wondering about the many aspects of the world, you will keep learning, and that will make you wiser in the long run. Maybe keeping that child-like wonder around is useful after all.

item.title: Moving sculpture aims to show how everything is interconnected
item.description:
Score 2 | Comments 2 (thread link) | @lhuser123
October 27, 2024 | https://www.tomlawton.com/wonder | archive.org

Big Wonder residency at Camp Kerala

Documentary by Chris Ramsay - magician and curator of rare & unusual objects

Wonder is available in three limited edition sizes.

WONDER

Quinessential art piece for home and studio

20cm polished copper spiral | Matt black aluminium turntable

Presently unavailable

BIG WONDER

Showcase art piece for transforming space

45cm polished copper spiral | Walnut/matt black turntable

Presently unavailable

GIANT WONDER

Colossal art piece for an extrordinary space

100cm spiral cast in aluminium - finished in polished silver or gold

Bepoke plinth made to order

1 of 2 rare giant Wonders to ever be made

Price on application

Please email enquiries to [email protected]

(free download)

Download WonderAR App on iPhone & Android to visualise Wonder in your space.

Big Wonder in polished copper with a walnut base

Wonder was imagined and designed in the years leading up to, then fabricated by Tom Lawton through the course of the Covid pandemic and with thanks to a successful crowdfunding campaign and a donation from the James Dyson Foundation it was first produced for public display in Malmesbury Abbey.

Comprising of a single, self-supporting, ribbon-like structure finished in polished copper, which appears to flow like water as it spirals both upwards and down, expanding outwards and contracting in.

Wonder arrived at Malmesbury Abbey to great reception and together with Malmesbury Live Arts and the Abbey, Tom organised a musical extravaganza 'Renaissance of Wonder' to celebrate its unveiling.

Hundreds & thousands of vistors have now visited the abbey to experience Wonder's universally peaceful and calming effect.

Reverend Oliver Ross, Malmesbury Abbey

Sign up to stay in the loop

Subscribe to newsletter

Wonder follows Uplift and began its life as a discrete and illuminating installation off Malmesbury high street in the cold winter of the third lockdown of the pandemic to serve as a provision of hope for the local community. Residents would often gather outside the window alone, with children, with elderly relatives and after long shifts at work.

The genesis of Wonder began in the years leading up to 2020. All Wonders are manufactured in the UK.

Since being unveiled and launched, Wonder has received hundreds of direct sales and Big Wonder has generated multiple commissions including being selected as the master illusion for the Museum of Illusions in various sites including their flagship location in Las Vegas, as well as showcase locations in San Diego, Seattle and Copenhagen.

Wonder brings an etherial and calming presence to a space, creating an atmosphere and focal point for relaxation, contemplation & meditation.

Wonder's impact on the public is already profound with hundreds of positive impressions and incredible interpretations from visitors far and wide. Some people are moved to dance, some to song, others to a state of deep calm and some are even moved to tears. The experience is universally uplifting and peaceful, just read the thousands of comments on these threads:

Reddit

Timmy Mallet's Facebook

Massimo on Twitter

Grayson Perry's Art Club

Follow @tomlawton on Instagram or Twitter and Uplifting Products on Facebook and Instagram for the latest news and product launches.

Wonder is also protected by five registered designs and has international patents pending. All rights reserved.
Images my not be used without prior written permission.
